Instability of the magnetohydrodynamics system at small but finite Reynolds number

Abstract

The aim of this paper is to give a result concerning the stability properties of the solutions of magnetohydrodynamics equations at small but finite Reynolds numbers. These solutions are found using the α\alpha-effect: this method gives us solutions which are highly oscillating spatially on the scale of the underlying flow but are growing on a larger scale depending on a parameter ε\varepsilon. We prove instability results for a dense subset of initial velocity field of the flow at given Reynolds number.

{keywords}

magnetohydrodynamics, stability, α\alpha-effect

1 Introduction

Dynamo theory first interested physicists almost one century ago, when Sir Joseph Larmor [14] wondered how a magnetic field could be generated by a rotating body like the Sun or the Earth. Since then, many results have come, both in mathematics and physics, to understand this kind of phenomena.

The physical model behind them is a coupled system derived from the interaction of a conductive fluid, which follows Navier-Stokes equations, and an electromagnetic field, which follows Maxwell equations and Ohm’s law. The interaction of the two physic quantities comes from the fact that a magnetic field has an effect on a moving conductive fluid, which creates in return a magnetic field. This kind of system is known as magnetohydrodynamics (MHD).

There are mainly two outcomes for MHD systems: the magnetic energy can either collapse (exponentially), or stay/grow. In the latter case we say we have a dynamo, and it is the effect we observe in bodies like the Sun. However, the understanding of dynamo mechanisms is not simple. Indeed, the most “intuitive” way we imagine the conductive fluid in rotation and the magnetic field (that is a 2D rotating fluid in the kernel, and a magnetic field that looks like the one of a static magnet) is actually a well known anti-dynamo situation. Anti-dynamo theorems have been widely studied, and some summary of the knowledge in the domain has been made in [11].

The kind of situation we want to study there is that of the second kind, that is dynamo situation (and more precisely growth). Positive results began to emerge only later in the 50’s, even though it was already well known that it is what occured in the Sun. In the 90’s M.M. Vishik [23] proved that fast dynamos (i.e. exponential growth) require Lagrangian chaos in the fluid. Those results spread the idea that the velocity field has to be chaotic enough to expect a dynamo effect. Because of this “negative” result, different methods were tried to find instability results, linked to singularities: Y.B. Ponomarenko [17] studied concentration phenomena to get dynamo result in the case where Laplace force is neglected (i.e. imposed velocity field) and his results were extended by Gilbert [10] and successfully experimentaly checked [6]. More realistic case of the Ponomarenko dynamo was studied by D. Gérard-Varet and F. Rousset [9]. All those results give only asymptotic results.

In this paper we will focus on another singular dynamo mechanism, called alpha effect, first introduced by E.N. Parker [16], which is based on scale separation: we formally decompose the magnetic and the velocity fields into two parts: a fluctuating part, evolving on a turbulent scale, and a mean part, evolving on a larger scale. The mean value is broadly the spatial average over a sphere of radius much larger than the typical distance on which the field is turbulent, but much smaller thant the distance on which we want to observe the dynamo effect (in what follows, these distances will be 11 and 1/ε1/\varepsilon, so scale separation will take place at small ε\varepsilon). Basically, this gives a decomposition of the velocity and magnetic fields under the form

u=u~​(x,x/ε,t)+u¯​(x,t),b=b~​(x,x/ε,t)+b¯​(x,t),\begin{split}u&=\tilde{u}(x,x/\varepsilon,t)+\bar{u}(x,t),\\ b&=\tilde{b}(x,x/\varepsilon,t)+\bar{b}(x,t),\\ \end{split} (1)

where u~\tilde{u} and b~\tilde{b} have null mean value on the second variable. The idea behind alpha effect is that the averaged induction term OPEN∇∧(u~∧b~CLOSE¯)\overline{\nabla\wedge(\tilde{u}\wedge\tilde{b}}) (we will specify those notations right below) that will appear in the MHD equations will permit us to obtain a destabilizing effect on the magnetic field.

The alpha effect was first formally studied by G.O. Roberts [19, 18], in the framework of periodic flows. His results were discussed by H.K. Moffatt [15], S. Childress [2] and A.M. Soward [20] that considered a larger class of velocity fields and range of parameters. This effect has been since experimentaly confirmed by R. Stieglitz and U. Müller [21].

The aim of the present paper is to provide a rigorous justification of this mechanism, in a nonlinear framework. We will improve substantially former results of D. Gérard-Varet [7, 8].

Before stating more precisely our results, we will first recall the system we will work with:

The generation of magnetic field BB by an electrically conducting fluid of velocity UU and magnetic diffusivity νm\nu_{m} follows the equations

{∂tB−∇∧(U∧B)−νm​Δ​B=0,∇⋅B=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}B-\nabla\wedge(U\wedge B)-\nu_{m}\Delta B=0,\\ \nabla\cdot B=0.\end{array}\right. (2)

These equations are derived from the Maxwell’s equation and Ohm’s law (see second section of [3], or [11] for more detailed derivation). Since other relevant physics quantities that appear in the Maxwell’s equations can be obtained from BB, it is enough to work with only that.

Furthermore, the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations that drive the evolution of the conducting fluid under the force created by the magnetic field write

{ρ​∂tU+ρ​U⋅∇U=−∇p+η​Δ​U+1μ0​(∇∧B)∧B+f,∇⋅u=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\rho\partial_{t}U+\rho U\cdot\nabla U=-\nabla p+\eta\Delta U+\frac{1}{\mu_{0}}(\nabla\wedge B)\wedge B+f,\\ \nabla\cdot u=0,\end{array}\right. (3)

where pp is the pressure field, ff is an additional forcing term, ρ\rho is the fluid mass density and η\eta is the fluid shear viscosity (see [3] again, keeping in mind the incompressible condition). The additional forcing term will be chosen to generate some steady velocity field (and thus will be independent of time), see below.

We study there oscillating field UU of amplitude VV, oscillating on a space-scale LL, and with magnetic diffusivity νm\nu_{m}. After proper nondimensionalization of time, space, pressure and magnetic field, we then have the full incompressible MHD system:

{∂tB−∇∧(u∧B)−1Rm​Δ​B=0,∂tU+U⋅∇U+∇p−1Re​Δ​U=(∇∧B)∧B+f,∇⋅B=0,∇⋅U=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}B-\nabla\wedge(u\wedge B)-\frac{1}{R_{m}}\Delta B=0,\\ \partial_{t}U+U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla p-\frac{1}{R_{e}}\Delta U=(\nabla\wedge B)\wedge B+f,\\ \nabla\cdot B=0,\\ \nabla\cdot U=0,\\ \end{array}\right. (4)

where Rm=L​VνmR_{m}=\frac{LV}{\nu_{m}} is the magnetic Reynolds number, and Re=ρ​L​VηR_{e}=\frac{\rho LV}{\eta} is the hydrodynamic Reynolds number.

Here we want to find a growing solution on a larger scale L/εL/\varepsilon (where ε>0\varepsilon>0), using the alpha effect introduced earlier. We will search this solution as a perturbation (ub)\begin{pmatrix}u\\ b\end{pmatrix} of a solution (Us0)\begin{pmatrix}U_{s}\\ 0\end{pmatrix} of this system (and the forcing term ff is chosen accordingly so that UsU_{s} is a solution of the Navier-Stokes equation):

{U=u+Us,B=b+0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}U=u+U_{s},\\ B=b+0.\end{array}\right. (5)

and the system in terms of bb, uu and UsU_{s} becomes

{∂tu+u⋅∇Us+Us⋅∇u−1Re​Δ​u+∇p=(∇∧b)∧b−u⋅∇u,∂tb−∇∧(Us∧b)−∇∧(u∧b)−1Rm​Δ​b=0,∇⋅b=0,∇⋅u=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla U_{s}+U_{s}\cdot\nabla u-\frac{1}{R_{e}}\Delta u+\nabla p=(\nabla\wedge b)\wedge b-u\cdot\nabla u,\\ \partial_{t}b-\nabla\wedge(U_{s}\wedge b)-\nabla\wedge(u\wedge b)-\frac{1}{R_{m}}\Delta b=0,\\ \nabla\cdot b=0,\\ \nabla\cdot u=0.\end{array}\right. (6)

The space variables for this system is denoted θ\theta, and corresponds to the fluctuation scale LL, 11 after non-dimensionalization. In particular, we assume that

Us=Us​(θ)∈\mc​C∞​(\mb​T3)U_{s}=U_{s}(\theta)\in\mc C^{\infty}(\mb T^{3}) (7)

and has zero-mean.

Later on, we shall introduce a larger scale variable x=ε​θx=\varepsilon\theta corresponding to the large scale L/εL/\varepsilon of the growing field.

Our main result is an instability theorem in the Liapunov sense for system (6). To state our result, we introduce the set \mc​H0∞​(\mb​T3)\mc H_{0}^{\infty}(\mb T^{3}) with his usual distance:

d⁡(U,U′)=∑k=0∞max⁡(1,‖U−U′‖\mc​Hk)2k,d(U,U^{\prime})=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\max\left(1,\|U-U^{\prime}\|_{\mc H^{k}}\right)}{2^{k}}, (8)

which makes it a Fréchet-space.

For T=(T1,T2,T3)∈(\mb​R+∗)3T=(T_{1},T_{2},T_{3})\in(\mb R_{+}^{*})^{3}, we denote

\mc​HTs=\mc​Hs​(\mb​R/T1​\mb​Z×\mb​R/T2​\mb​Z×\mb​R/T3​\mb​Z)\mc H_{T}^{s}=\mc H^{s}(\mb R/T_{1}\mb Z\times\mb R/T_{2}\mb Z\times\mb R/T_{3}\mb Z) (9)

the Sobolev space of order ss on the torus

\mb​R/T1​\mb​Z×\mb​R/T2​\mb​Z×\mb​R/T3​\mb​Z.\mb R/T_{1}\mb Z\times\mb R/T_{2}\mb Z\times\mb R/T_{3}\mb Z. (10)

We have the following theorem: {theoreme} Let s>5/2s>5/2 be a real number. There exists a dense subset \ms​P\ms P of the unit ball of \mc​H0∞​(\mb​T3)\mc H_{0}^{\infty}(\mb T^{3}) and Rm0>0R_{m}^{0}>0 such that for all Us∈\ms​PU_{s}\in\ms P and Rm<Rm0R_{m}<R_{m}^{0}, for all Re>0R_{e}>0, the solution (Us0)\begin{pmatrix}U_{s}\\ 0\end{pmatrix} of the (MHD) system is nonlinearly unstable in the following sense:

There exists T=(T1,T2,T3)∈(\mb​N∗)3T=(T_{1},T_{2},T_{3})\in(\mb N^{*})^{3} and initial values

(u0b0)∈\mc​HTs,\begin{pmatrix}u_{0}\\ b_{0}\end{pmatrix}\in\mc H_{T}^{s}, (11)

and C0>0C_{0}>0 such that for all δ>0\delta>0, the solution (uδbδ)\begin{pmatrix}u_{\delta}\\ b_{\delta}\end{pmatrix} of (6) with initial value δ​(u0b0)\delta\begin{pmatrix}u_{0}\\ b_{0}\end{pmatrix} satisfies

‖(uδbδ)⁡(tδ)‖\mc​HTs≥C0\left\|\begin{pmatrix}u_{\delta}\\ b_{\delta}\end{pmatrix}(t_{\delta})\right\|_{\mc H_{T}^{s}}\geq C_{0} (12)

for some time tδt_{\delta}. Furthermore, we have the estimate on tδt_{\delta} as δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0:

tδ∼δ→0−ln⁡δCt_{\delta}\sim_{\delta\rightarrow 0}-\frac{\ln\delta}{C} (13)

As expected, this theorem expresses the instability of the MHD system, up to consider a larger periodic box [0,T1]×[0,T2]×[0,T3][0,T_{1}]\times[0,T_{2}]\times[0,T_{3}]. Let us point out that (T1,T2,T3)∈(\mb​N∗)3(T_{1},T_{2},T_{3})\in(\mb N^{*})^{3}, so that UsU_{s} is also periodic on this larger scale.

In particular, for any

(u0b0)∈\mc​HTs,\begin{pmatrix}u_{0}\\ b_{0}\end{pmatrix}\in\mc H_{T}^{s}, (14)

and any δ>0\delta>0, system (6) has a unique solution

(uδbδ)∈\mc​C0​([0,T∗],HTs)\begin{pmatrix}u_{\delta}\\ b_{\delta}\end{pmatrix}\in\mc C^{0}([0,T^{*}],H_{T}^{s}) (15)

for some T∗>0T^{*}>0 with initial data δ​(u0,b0)\delta\begin{pmatrix}u_{0},b_{0}\end{pmatrix}. Moreover, for δ>0\delta>0 small enough, it is well-known that one can take T∗=+∞T^{*}=+\infty.

Up to our knowledge, our theorem is the first full justification of the α\alpha-effect, in the nonlinear context.

In particular, it extends substentially the article [7] by David Gérard-Varet. Recast in our variables, this article considers the case of large magnetic diffusion, that is Rm=ε≪1R_{m}=\varepsilon\ll 1. Briefly, it is shown that for all m∈\mb​Nm\in\mb N, there are solutions of (6) (on a larger box depending on ε\varepsilon) that go from amplitude εm\varepsilon^{m} initially to an amplitude η=η⁡(m)>0\eta=\eta(m)>0 independent of ε\varepsilon (but depending on mm).

Note that, as η\eta depends on mm, this result does not yield Liapunov instability at fixed small ε\varepsilon. Moreover, the study in [7] corresponds to vanishing magnetic Reynolds number. In our theorem, the threshold Rm0R_{m}^{0} is of order 11, which is much more satisfactory from a physical point of view.

The outline of the paper is as follow:

The first and main part of the paper is the constructino of an exact unstable eigenmode for the linearization of (6). It involves sharp spectral analysis arguments. Then, on the basis of this linear analysis, the proof of nonlinear instability is given in section 3.

2 Linear instability

In this section we will establish linear instability for the induction part of the MHD system. In other words, we will exhibit an unstable eigenmode of the linear operator

\fonction​[]​[b]​[∇∧(U∧b)−1Rm​Δ​b]\fonction[][b][\nabla\wedge(U\wedge b)-\frac{1}{R_{m}}\Delta b] (16)

for a large class of UU. This will be possible, through an accurate mathematical analysis of the alpha effect described in the introduction.

Let us write down the induction equation:

∂tb−∇∧(U∧b)−1Rm​Δ​b=0,∇⋅b=0,\begin{split}\partial_{t}b-\nabla\wedge(U\wedge b)-\frac{1}{R_{m}}\Delta b=0,\\ \nabla\cdot b=0,\end{split} (17)

where U∈\mc​H0∞​(\mb​T3)U\in\mc H_{0}^{\infty}(\mb T^{3}) is independent of time.

In this section we prove the following linear instability result: {theoreme} Let s≥0s\geq 0 be a real number. There exists a dense subset \ms​P\ms P of the unit ball of \mc​H0∞​(\mb​T3)\mc H_{0}^{\infty}(\mb T^{3}) and a positive real Rm0R_{m}^{0} such that for all positive Rm<Rm0R_{m}<R_{m}^{0}, and all U∈\ms​PU\in\ms P, there exists ξ∈\mb​(2​π​\mb​Q∗)3\xi\in\mb(2\pi\mb Q^{*})^{3} and a number ε0>0\varepsilon_{0}>0 such that for all 0<ε<ε00<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{0}, there exists a solution BB of (17) of the form

b⁡(t,θ)=e\iim​ε​ξ⋅θ​eλε​t​bε​(θ)b(t,\theta)=e^{\iim\varepsilon\xi\cdot\theta}e^{\lambda^{\varepsilon}t}b^{\varepsilon}(\theta) (18)

where bε∈\mc​Hs​(\mb​T3)b^{\varepsilon}\in\mc H^{s}(\mb T^{3}), with exponential growth when t→+∞t\rightarrow+\infty (that is ℜ⁡(λε)>0\Re(\lambda^{\varepsilon})>0).

2.1 Linearized equation

Let U∈\mc​H0∞​(\mb​T3)U\in\mc H_{0}^{\infty}(\mb T^{3}) be a spatially periodic velocity field in \mb​R3\mb R^{3} (of period 11).

Since we will look for the growth of the magnetic field on a larger space-scale 1/ε1/\varepsilon, we will directly look for a solution bb under the form

b⁡(θ,t)=Bε​(ε​θ,θ,ε​t)=B¯ε​(ε​θ,ε​t)+B~ε​(ε​θ,θ,ε​t),b(\theta,t)=B^{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon\theta,\theta,\varepsilon t)=\bar{B}^{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon\theta,\varepsilon t)+\tilde{B}^{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon\theta,\theta,\varepsilon t), (19)

where Bε=Bε​(x,θ,t)B^{\varepsilon}=B^{\varepsilon}(x,\theta,t) depends both on the original variable θ\theta and a slow variable x=ε​θx=\varepsilon\theta. One can decompose BεB^{\varepsilon} as the sum of a large-scale field B¯ε\bar{B}^{\varepsilon} which doesn’t depend on the smaller variable, and a small-scale zero-mean-value field B~ε\tilde{B}^{\varepsilon}, i.e. ∫\mb​T3B~ε​(x,θ,t)​\ud​θ=0\int_{\mb T^{3}}\tilde{B}^{\varepsilon}(x,\theta,t)\ud\theta=0, as suggested in the introduction.

In view of (4), the new field BεB^{\varepsilon} should satisfy (dropping the prime over time variable tt):

{∂tBε−∇x∧(U∧Bε)−1ε​∇θ∧(U∧Bε)−εRm​Δx​Bε−1ε​Rm​Δθ​Bε−2Rm​∑i=1d∂xi​θiBε=0,∇x⋅Bε+1ε​∇θ⋅Bε=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}B^{\varepsilon}-\nabla_{x}\wedge(U\wedge B^{\varepsilon})-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge B^{\varepsilon})-\frac{\varepsilon}{R_{m}}\Delta_{x}B^{\varepsilon}-\frac{1}{\varepsilon R_{m}}\Delta_{\theta}B^{\varepsilon}-\frac{2}{R_{m}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{x_{i}\theta_{i}}B^{\varepsilon}=0,\\ \nabla_{x}\cdot B^{\varepsilon}+\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\nabla_{\theta}\cdot B^{\varepsilon}=0.\end{array}\right. (20)

Bε=e\iim​ξ⋅x​Bε′​(t,θ).B^{\varepsilon}=e^{\iim\xi\cdot x}{B^{\varepsilon}}^{\prime}(t,\theta). (21)

Dropping the prime again, we get:

{∂tBε−\iim​ξ∧(U∧Bε)−1ε​∇θ∧(U∧Bε)+εRm​ξ2​Bε−1ε​Rm​Δθ​Bε−2Rm​\iim​∑i=1dξi​∂θiBε=0,\iim​ξ⋅Bε+1ε​∇θ⋅Bε=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}B^{\varepsilon}-\iim\xi\wedge(U\wedge B^{\varepsilon})-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge B^{\varepsilon})+\frac{\varepsilon}{R_{m}}\xi^{2}B^{\varepsilon}-\frac{1}{\varepsilon R_{m}}\Delta_{\theta}B^{\varepsilon}-\frac{2}{R_{m}}\iim\sum_{i=1}^{d}\xi_{i}\partial_{\theta_{i}}B^{\varepsilon}=0,\\ \iim\xi\cdot B^{\varepsilon}+\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\nabla_{\theta}\cdot B^{\varepsilon}=0.\end{array}\right. (22)

We denote by Aε=A0+ε​A1+ε2​A2A^{\varepsilon}=A^{0}+\varepsilon A^{1}+\varepsilon^{2}A^{2} the operator associated to the first equation of (22), that is

A0=∇θ∧(U∧⋅)+1RmΔθA1=\iimξ∧(U∧⋅)+2Rm\iim∑i=1dξi∂θiA2=−1Rm​ξ2​\Id,\begin{split}A^{0}&=\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\cdot)+\frac{1}{R_{m}}\Delta_{\theta}\\ A^{1}&=\iim\xi\wedge(U\wedge\cdot)+\frac{2}{R_{m}}\iim\sum_{i=1}^{d}\xi_{i}\partial_{\theta_{i}}\\ A^{2}&=-\frac{1}{R_{m}}\xi^{2}\Id,\\ \end{split} (23)

∂tBε=1ε​Aε​Bε.\partial_{t}B^{\varepsilon}=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}A^{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon}. (24)

We want to find a solution in power series of ε\varepsilon of that equation of type

Bε​(θ,t)=eλε​t​B0ε​(θ).B^{\varepsilon}(\theta,t)=e^{\lambda^{\varepsilon}t}B_{0}^{\varepsilon}(\theta). (25)

2.2 Study of the first term in the development

The first equation, corresponding to ε=0\varepsilon=0, writes

A0​B00=0,A^{0}B_{0}^{0}=0, (27)

that is 1Rm​Δθ​B00+∇θ∧(U∧B00)=0\frac{1}{R_{m}}\Delta_{\theta}B_{0}^{0}+\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge B_{0}^{0})=0, which depends only on the independent variable θ\theta.

1Rm​Δθ​B~00+∇θ∧(U∧B~00)=−∇θ∧(U∧B¯00).\frac{1}{R_{m}}\Delta_{\theta}\tilde{B}_{0}^{0}+\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\tilde{B}_{0}^{0})=-\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\bar{B}_{0}^{0}). (28)

\fonction​Δθ​\mc​H0s+2​(\mb​T3)⊂\mc​H0s​(\mb​T3)​\mc​H0s​(\mb​T3)\fonction{\Delta_{\theta}}{\mc H_{0}^{s+2}(\mb T^{3})\subset\mc H_{0}^{s}(\mb T^{3})}{\mc H_{0}^{s}(\mb T^{3})} (29)

\fonctionΔθ−1∇θ∧(U∧⋅)\mcH0s(\mbT3)\mcH0s+1(\mbT3)⊂\mcH0s(\mbT3)\fonction{\Delta_{\theta}^{-1}\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\cdot)}{\mc H_{0}^{s}(\mb T^{3})}{\mc H_{0}^{s+1}(\mb T^{3})\subset\mc H_{0}^{s}(\mb T^{3})} (30)

Thus, by classical result on the spectrum of compact operators, the operator

LRm=1RmΔθ⋅+∇θ∧(U∧⋅)=Δθ(1Rm\Id+Δθ−1∇θ∧(U∧⋅))L_{R_{m}}=\frac{1}{R_{m}}\Delta_{\theta}\cdot+\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\cdot)=\Delta_{\theta}(\frac{1}{R_{m}}\Id+\Delta_{\theta}^{-1}\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\cdot)) (31)

is invertible as an operator from \mc​H0s+2​(\mb​T3)\mc H_{0}^{s+2}(\mb T^{3}) to \mc​H0s​(\mb​T3)\mc H_{0}^{s}(\mb T^{3}) but for some countable set CLC_{L} of RmR_{m} which can be written as a sequence of numbers growing to +∞+\infty. In particular it is invertible for RmR_{m} smaller than a given value Rm0R_{m}^{0}.

Since −∇θ∧(U∧B¯00)∈\mc​H0s​(\mb​T3)-\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\bar{B}_{0}^{0})\in\mc H_{0}^{s}(\mb T^{3}) for any B¯00∈\mb​R3\bar{B}_{0}^{0}\in\mb R^{3}, the equation (28) admits exactly one solution for every B¯00∈\mb​R3\bar{B}_{0}^{0}\in\mb R^{3}. Then for any RmR_{m} out of CLC_{L}, the equation

LRm​B~00=−∇θ∧(U∧B¯00)L_{R_{m}}\tilde{B}_{0}^{0}=-\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\bar{B}_{0}^{0}) (32)

is equivalent to

B~00=\ms​L​(θ)​B¯00.\tilde{B}_{0}^{0}=\ms L(\theta)\bar{B}_{0}^{0}. (33)

where \ms​L​(θ)\ms L(\theta) is the operator from \mb​R3\mb R^{3} to \mc​H0s+2​(\mb​T3)\mc H_{0}^{s+2}(\mb T^{3}) defined by

\msL(θ)=−LRm−1∇θ∧(U∧⋅)\ms L(\theta)=-L_{R_{m}}^{-1}\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\cdot) (34)

That means that the A0A^{0} operator has a kernel of dimension 33, \fonction​A0​\mc​Hs+2​(\mb​T3)⊂\mc​Hs​(\mb​T3)​\mc​Hs​(\mb​T3)\fonction{A^{0}}{\mc H^{s+2}(\mb T^{3})\subset\mc H^{s}(\mb T^{3})}{\mc H^{s}(\mb T^{3})}, that is ker⁡A0={B¯+\ms​L​(θ)​B¯,B¯∈\mb​R3}\ker A^{0}=\{\bar{B}+\ms L(\theta)\bar{B},\bar{B}\in\mb R^{3}\}.

1RmΔ+∇θ∧(U∧⋅)−λ\Id=A0−λ\Id\frac{1}{R_{m}}\Delta+\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\cdot)-\lambda\Id=A^{0}-\lambda\Id (35)

is invertible for large enough λ\lambda if seen as an operator from \mc​H0s+2\mc H_{0}^{s+2} to \mc​H0s\mc H_{0}^{s}. Thus the resolvant of A0A^{0} is compact in at least one λ\lambda, and all spectral projections are of finite dimension, that is A0A^{0} has eigenvalues of finite dimension, isolated and they are the only spectral values of A0A^{0} (see [13] p.187).

Let σ\sigma be a smooth path surrounding 00 and no other eigenvalue of A0A^{0}. For ε\varepsilon sufficiently small, since AεA^{\varepsilon} varies continuously on ε\varepsilon, σ\sigma doesn’t cross the spectrum of AεA^{\varepsilon}, and the operator

∑k≠0U^j​(−k)∧V^i​(k)​(\iim​k|k|2⋅B)=0,\sum_{k\neq 0}\hat{U}^{j}(-k)\wedge\hat{V}^{i}(k)\left(\iim\frac{k}{|k|^{2}}\cdot B\right)=0, (66)

and then

α(2)​(U~)=α(2)​(Uj)−δ1j+1​(000010001)−δ2j+2​(100000001)−δ3j+3​(100010000),\alpha^{(2)}(\tilde{U})=\alpha^{(2)}(U^{j})-\frac{\delta_{1}}{j+1}\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}-\frac{\delta_{2}}{j+2}\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&0&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}-\frac{\delta_{3}}{j+3}\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix}, (67)

where the δi\delta_{i} can be chosen as small as we want. Thus α(2)​(U)\alpha^{(2)}(U) is as near as we want from a matrix of distinct non-zero eigenvalues, and it’s the same for αS​(U)\alpha^{S}(U) for Rm<Rm0R_{m}<R_{m}^{0} (NB: the set in which RmR_{m} can be taken will vary continuously with UU, thus the precaution we took at the beginning of the subsection to be sufficiently far from the limit)

2.5.3 End of the proof

In the sequel of this subsection, we now work with U~\tilde{U} instead of UU, droping the tilda. Thus, αS\alpha^{S} has distinct non-zero eigenvalues. In Fourier transform, we now have to find the eigenvalues of the matrix Aξ​αA+Aξ​αSA^{\xi}\alpha^{A}+A^{\xi}\alpha^{S}, where

Aξ=\iim​(0−ξ3ξ2ξ30−ξ1−ξ2ξ10).A^{\xi}=\iim\begin{pmatrix}0&-\xi_{3}&\xi_{2}\\ \xi_{3}&0&-\xi_{1}\\ -\xi_{2}&\xi_{1}&0\end{pmatrix}. (68)

Let there be P∈\ms​O3​(\mb​R)P\in\ms O_{3}(\mb R) such that

Pt​αS​P=(α1000α2000α3)=D,{}^{t}P\alpha^{S}P=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha_{1}&0&0\\ 0&\alpha_{2}&0\\ 0&0&\alpha_{3}\end{pmatrix}=D, (69)

and write ζ=Pt​ξ\zeta={}^{t}P\xi. The matrix Aζ​DA^{\zeta}D has λ0=0\lambda_{0}=0 eigenvalue, and two opposite eigenvalues given by

λ±=±ζ12​α2​α3+ζ22​α3​α1+ζ32​α1​α2.\lambda_{\pm}=\pm\sqrt{\zeta_{1}^{2}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}+\zeta_{2}^{2}\alpha_{3}\alpha_{1}+\zeta_{3}^{2}\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}. (70)

Those eigenvalues are real for any ζ\zeta if all eigenvalues of αS\alpha^{S} have the same sign. Otherwise, there exists a cone with vertex 00 outside of which they are. Furthermore, for ζ\zeta in the complement Ω\Omega of this cone, λ+\lambda_{+} stays positive, and λ−\lambda_{-} stays negative. Thus, the eigenvectors of Aζ​DA^{\zeta}D depend regularly of ζ\zeta. From now on, we fix some ζ\zeta in this good set Ω\Omega. We can also assume that ξ=P​ζ∈(2​π​\mb​Q+∗)3\xi=P\zeta\in(2\pi\mb Q_{+}^{*})^{3}.

Let β\beta be an eigenvector associated to λ+\lambda_{+}. Then Aζ​D​β=\iim​ζ∧(D​β)=λ+​βA^{\zeta}D\beta=\iim\zeta\wedge(D\beta)=\lambda_{+}\beta, so ζ⋅β=0\zeta\cdot\beta=0. Thus, we have Aζ​Pt​αA​P​β=ζ∧(γ∧β)=−\iim​(ζ⋅γ)​βA^{\zeta}{}^{t}P\alpha^{A}P\beta=\zeta\wedge(\gamma\wedge\beta)=-\iim(\zeta\cdot\gamma)\beta, where γ\gamma is a vector such that ∀b∈\mb​R3,Pt​αA​P​b=γ∧b\forall b\in\mb R^{3},{}^{t}P\alpha^{A}Pb=\gamma\wedge b. Thus β\beta is also an eigenvector of Aζ​Pt​αA​PA^{\zeta}{}^{t}P\alpha^{A}P, associated with the eigenvalue −\iim​(ζ⋅γ)-\iim(\zeta\cdot\gamma).

Now changing back to ξ=P​ζ\xi=P\zeta, we have that

Aζ=Pt​Aξ​P,A^{\zeta}={}^{t}PA^{\xi}P, (71)

so that β\beta is an eigenvector of Pt​Aξ​αA​P+Pt​Aξ​P​D{}^{t}PA^{\xi}\alpha^{A}P+{}^{t}PA^{\xi}PD associated to the eigenvalue λ+−\iim​(ζ⋅γ)=λ+−\iim​(ξ⋅P​γ)\lambda_{+}-\iim(\zeta\cdot\gamma)=\lambda_{+}-\iim(\xi\cdot P\gamma). And thus P​βP\beta is an eigenvector of Aξ​αA+Aξ​αSA^{\xi}\alpha^{A}+A^{\xi}\alpha^{S} associated to an eigenvalue of positive real part, that is a growing mode solution of the first term of (41).

2.6 Conclusion to the linear case

We have proven now the existence of an eigenvector b00b^{0}_{0} of the equation

P0​A1​P0​Bε+ε​A′ε​Bε=λε​BεP^{0}A^{1}P^{0}B^{\varepsilon}+\varepsilon{A^{\prime}}^{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon}=\lambda^{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon} (72)

for ε=0\varepsilon=0 with positive real part, that is an exponentially-growing mode of the form

Bε​(x,θ,t)=b00​(θ,ζ)​e(λ+−\iim​ζ⋅γ)​t+\iim​ζ⋅xB^{\varepsilon}(x,\theta,t)=b^{0}_{0}(\theta,\zeta)e^{(\lambda_{+}-\iim\zeta\cdot\gamma)t+\iim\zeta\cdot x} (73)

of the induction equation for given velocity field UsU_{s} and small enough RmR_{m} (and ε=0\varepsilon=0). Since the operator 1ε​Pε​Aε​Pε\frac{1}{\varepsilon}P^{\varepsilon}A^{\varepsilon}P^{\varepsilon} varies analytically on ε\varepsilon for small ε\varepsilon, and has distinct eigenvalues for ε=0\varepsilon=0, so do eigenvalues and eigenvectors of this operator, and thus the result remains valid when ε\varepsilon is positive sufficiently small (at fixed ξ\xi), and we have now an eigenvector b0b_{0} of the induction equation for small enough ε\varepsilon.

This concludes the proof of theorem 2.

{remarque}

Most of what we said stays valid if we take RmR_{m} out of a discrete set of values instead of only “small enough”. Only the fact that α⁡(U)\alpha(U) is as near as we want to a matrix of distinct non-zero eigenvalues remains a problem in that case.

Pondering on theorem 2, we will prove in the next section the instability of the full nonlinear (MHD) system (4).

3 Nonlinear instability

We will now prove nonlinear instability of the system (4). For that we will adapt a method developped by S. Friedlander, W. Strauss and M. Vishik in [5] (itself adapted from Y. Guo and W. Strauss in [12]) to prove nonlinear instability given linear instability. The condition s>3/2+1s>3/2+1 in the main theorem is used only in this section to obtain an inequality on the nonlinear terms similar to that in the article. Actually, using the parabolic feature of the MHD system, it would be possible to lower our regularity requirements (see for instance Friedlander et al [4] in the context of the Navier-Stokes equations). We stick here to regular data for simplicity of exposure.

Let Us∈\ms​PU_{s}\in\ms P belonging to the dense subset of linearly unstable flows described in the previous section.

We introduce Leray operator \mb​P\mb P to get rid of pp. We rewrite system (6) as

∂t\ms​U+Ls​\ms​U=Q⁡(\ms​U,\ms​U),\partial_{t}\ms U+L_{s}\ms U=Q(\ms U,\ms U), (74)

where

\ms​U=(ub),\ms U=\begin{pmatrix}u\\ b\end{pmatrix}, (75)
Ls​\ms​U=(\mb​P​(u⋅∇Us+Us⋅∇u)−1Re​Δ​u−∇∧(Us∧b)−1RmΔb)L_{s}\ms U=\begin{pmatrix}\mb P(u\cdot\nabla U_{s}+U_{s}\cdot\nabla u)-\frac{1}{R_{e}}\Delta u\\ -\nabla\wedge(U_{s}\wedge b)-\frac{1}{R_{m}}\Delta b\end{pmatrix} (76)

is the linearized operator around (Us0)\begin{pmatrix}U_{s}\\ 0\end{pmatrix}, and

Q⁡(\ms​U,\ms​U)=(\mb​P​(∇∧b∧b−u⋅∇u)∇∧(u∧b))Q(\ms U,\ms U)=\begin{pmatrix}\mb P(\nabla\wedge b\wedge b-u\cdot\nabla u)\\ \nabla\wedge(u\wedge b)\end{pmatrix} (77)

is the nonlinearity.

We shall consider this system in \mc​HTs\mc H_{T}^{s}, TT to be specified later. We also denote LT2L^{2}_{T} the L2L^{2} space on the torus. Since we will work in these spaces until the end of the proof, we will drop the TT in the notation. We have the following a priori estimates for the nonlinear term:

Every term of every component of Q⁡(\ms​U,\ms​U)Q(\ms U,\ms U) can be written as a product of one component of \ms​U\ms U and one of ∇\msU\nabla\ms U (composed by \mb​P\mb P). Thus, we have the first estimate

∥Q(\msU,\msU)∥L2≤C∥\msU⋅∇\msU∥L2≤C∥\msU∥L2∥∇\msU∥L∞.\|Q(\ms U,\ms U)\|_{L^{2}}\leq C\|\ms U\cdot\nabla\ms U\|_{L^{2}}\leq C\|\ms U\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla\ms U\|_{L^{\infty}}. (78)

For r=12​(s+n/2+1)>n/2+1r=\frac{1}{2}(s+n/2+1)>n/2+1 (here n=3n=3), we have that

∥∇\msU∥L∞≤∥\msU∥\mc​Hr,\|\nabla\ms U\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|\ms U\|_{\mc H^{r}}, (79)

and

‖\ms​U‖\mc​Hr≤C​‖\ms​U‖L2η​‖\ms​U‖\mc​Hs1−η\|\ms U\|_{\mc H^{r}}\leq C\|\ms U\|_{L^{2}}^{\eta}\|\ms U\|_{\mc H^{s}}^{1-\eta} (80)

for η\eta such that r=(1−η)​sr=(1-\eta)s (i.e. η=12−n+24​s=12−54​s\eta=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{n+2}{4s}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{5}{4s}).

Thus, we have:

‖Q⁡(\ms​U,\ms​U)‖L2≤C​‖\ms​U‖L21+η​‖\ms​U‖\mc​Hs1−η\|Q(\ms U,\ms U)\|_{L^{2}}\leq C\|\ms U\|_{L^{2}}^{1+\eta}\|\ms U\|_{\mc H^{s}}^{1-\eta} (81)

We shall prove the following theorem, which is a mere reformulation of the first theorem: {theoreme} Suppose s>3/2+1s>3/2+1, RmR_{m} small enough and Re>0R_{e}>0. Then there exists a vector T=(T1,T2,T3)T=(T_{1},T_{2},T_{3}) with integer coordinates such that the system (74) is nonlinearly unstable in \mc​HTs\mc H_{T}^{s} in the following sense:

There exists a growing mode \ms​U0=(u0b0)\ms U_{0}=\begin{pmatrix}u_{0}\\ b_{0}\end{pmatrix} with ‖\ms​U0‖\mc​HTs=1\|\ms U_{0}\|_{\mc H_{T}^{s}}=1 of the linearized system and a constant C0>0C_{0}>0 depending only on \ms​U0,s,n,ρ\ms U_{0},s,n,\rho such that for all δ>0\delta>0, the perturbation of the linear solution δ​\ms​U0\delta\ms U_{0} satisfies ‖\ms​U​(tδ)‖\mc​HTs≥C0\|\ms U(t_{\delta})\|_{\mc H_{T}^{s}}\geq C_{0} for some time tδt_{\delta}. Furthermore, tδ∼δ→0−ln⁡δρt_{\delta}\sim_{\delta\rightarrow 0}-\frac{\ln\delta}{\rho}. {remarque} This theorem only proves that the solution reaches high values in finite time however small the initial condition is. In particular it doesn’t say wether it explodes in finite time or is defined for all time, since both situations are possible in the result of the theorem. Actually, for small enough initial data (that is small enough δ\delta), it is classical that the solution of the system doesn’t explode in finite time and thus the approximation of tδt_{\delta} for vanishing δ\delta is valid. More details in [22] (Theorem 3.8)

Assume in contrary that the system is nonlinearly stable while spectrally unstable, that is that for any growing mode of initial value \ms​U0=(u0b0)\ms U_{0}=\begin{pmatrix}u_{0}\\ b_{0}\end{pmatrix} with ‖\ms​U0‖\mc​HTs=1\|\ms U_{0}\|_{\mc H_{T}^{s}}=1 in any box TT of the system (i.e. an eigenvector of LsL_{s} associated to an eigenvalue with positive real part) and for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists a δ>0\delta>0 such that for all t>0t>0, the solution \ms​U​(t)\ms U(t) of the system with initial values δ​\ms​U0\delta\ms U_{0} satisfies ‖\ms​U​(t)‖\mc​HTs≤ε\|\ms U(t)\|_{\mc H_{T}^{s}}\leq\varepsilon.

belongs to \mb​N3\mb N^{3}. This is possible as ξ∈(2​π​\mb​Q+∗)3\xi\in(2\pi\mb Q_{+}^{*})^{3} (take ε\varepsilon to be the inverse of a large integer). {∂t\ms​U˙=Ls​\ms​U˙+Q⁡(\ms​U,\ms​U)\ms​U˙|t=0=0\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\dot{\ms U}=L_{s}\dot{\ms U}+Q(\ms U,\ms U)\\ \dot{\ms U}_{|t=0}=0\end{array}\right. (87)

where λ\lambda is the coefficient in the growing linear mode. Then, since we supposed that \ms​U=\ms​Ul+\ms​U˙\ms U=\ms U_{l}+\dot{\ms U} remains bounded, and ‖\ms​Ul‖∼δ​eρ​t​‖\ms​U0‖\|\ms U_{l}\|\sim\delta e^{\rho t}\|\ms U_{0}\|, we have that Tδ<∞T_{\delta}<\infty.

‖\ms​U˙​(t)‖L2≤Cη​∫0teρ​(1+η2)​(t−s)​‖\ms​U‖L21+η​‖\ms​U‖\mc​Hs1−η​\ud​s.\|\dot{\ms U}(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq C_{\eta}\int_{0}^{t}e^{\rho(1+\frac{\eta}{2})(t-s)}\|\ms U\|_{L^{2}}^{1+\eta}\|\ms U\|_{\mc H^{s}}^{1-\eta}\ud s. (91)

We will now estimate the time in which ‖\ms​U‖\mc​Hs\|\ms U\|_{\mc H^{s}} becomes of order 11. Denote by T0T_{0} this time:

T0=sup{t>0,∀s≤t,∥\msU(s)∥\mc​Hs≤1}.T_{0}=\sup\{t>0,\forall s\leq t,\|\ms U(s)\|_{\mc H^{s}}\leq 1\}. (99)

Tδ≥ln⁡(‖\ms​U0‖L22​C′​δη)​1η​ρT_{\delta}\geq\ln\left(\frac{\|\ms U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}}{2C^{\prime}\delta^{\eta}}\right)\frac{1}{\eta\rho} (101)
